title: Hunting deer and big game
summary: For a hunter who already owns a legal firearm or bow and has had basic training. Be sure of your target and what is beyond it. Take only a standing animal, broadside or quartering away, and aim just behind the front shoulder at the heart and lungs. After the shot, mark the spot and wait at least an hour before following, longer after a gut shot. In a tree stand, wear a full-body harness and stay connected the whole time. Drag the deer out, never carry it on your shoulders, and get help if it is too heavy.
doFirst: Be sure of your target and what is beyond it. If you can’t see what is beyond the target, don’t take the shot (NYS DEC, Maine hunter education).
In a tree stand: wear a full-body harness and stay connected from the time you leave the ground until you are back down (NYS DEC).

Shoot only a standing animal that is broadside or quartering away, within your range, and aim at the heart and lungs just behind the front shoulder (Texas Parks and Wildlife, New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). If the angle is wrong, wait or pass.
After the shot: watch where it goes, mark the last spot you saw it, and wait at least 1 hour before you follow it; after a gut shot, at least 6 to 8 hours (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Drag or cart the deer out, never on your shoulders (Missouri Department of Conservation). If it is too heavy for you, go and get help (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

blocks.p: This page assumes you already own a legal firearm or bow and have had basic training with it. It does not teach choosing a firearm or shooting. It covers what changes when the deer is food: making a clean kill, finding the animal, staying safe, and getting it out. Field dressing, butchering and keeping the meat have their own pages, linked at the end.
In normal times New York requires a hunting licence and sets seasons, hours, legal methods, orange clothing and tagging. They are all in New York rules.

blocks.label: New York rules for hunting, fishing and trapping

list: Tell someone where you will be hunting and when you will be back. A map showing your stand helps others find you if you are late (NYS DEC).
Never hunt alone if you can help it (American Heart Association).
Prepare for winter weather, and carry emergency supplies such as a flashlight, water and high-energy food (NYS DEC).
Don’t hunt on hot days unless you have a way to keep the meat cool (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). Cooling a deer is in Field dressing game.

blocks.p: After fallout, the caution for wild game is in Game, fish, milk and gardens after fallout: don’t use it until officials say you can.

sections.h: What changes when it is for food

list: A well-placed shot puts the animal down almost at once, damages little meat and makes field dressing easier (Connecticut hunter safety manual).

A gut shot does not kill quickly: the animal can escape and suffer, and the gut contents can spoil the meat (Connecticut hunter safety manual). A misplaced shot can mean a long, suffering animal and a deer you never find (Texas Parks and Wildlife).
A shot from the front can damage a lot of meat and pass through the stomach into a hind leg (Texas Parks and Wildlife).
Heat spoils meat: field dress the animal as soon as you can (Massachusetts hunter education).

Lead bullets leave small lead fragments in the meat that you cannot detect. Cornell Cooperative Extension suggests non-lead bullets or slugs; with lead, throw out the meat around the wound channel. Who should not eat game shot with lead is in Field dressing game.

sections.h: Your target and what is beyond it

blocks.p: NYS DEC’s firearm rules: treat every firearm as if it is loaded; keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction; keep your finger off the trigger until you are ready to fire; identify your target and what lies beyond it.

list: Never fire at a sound or at movement. Use binoculars to identify your target and what is behind it; never use your rifle scope as binoculars (Washington hunter education).
If you cannot see what lies beyond the target, don’t take the shot. Check for a safe backstop: something solid enough to stop the bullet that will not make it ricochet (Maine hunter education).
Bullets go a long way: a .22 bullet can travel over 1½ miles (2.4 km), a centerfire bullet several miles, and a slug over 800 yards (730 m) (Maine hunter education).
A small branch can deflect an arrow or a bullet (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Never wear the colour of any game animal in the area, and wear hunter orange so others know you are a hunter (Washington hunter education).

blocks.p: The vital area is the heart and lungs in the chest; the liver and the big blood vessels are vital too (Texas Parks and Wildlife, Massachusetts bowhunter education). The best shot passes through both lungs (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

steps: Wait for the animal to stand still. Shoot only an animal that is standing still and unaware of you, within your effective range (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife), and don’t shoot at a moving deer (Connecticut hunter safety manual).
Wait for it to turn broadside: side-on, it shows the biggest target for the heart and lungs, and it is the best shot for anyone new (Texas Parks and Wildlife).

Aim just behind the shoulder. Follow the back edge of the front leg nearest you up into the body, and aim about one third of the way up from the bottom of the chest (Texas Parks and Wildlife, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
Pick one small spot there, smaller than a pie plate. Don’t aim at the whole animal (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

Quartering away (rear end angled away from you): aim at the front shoulder on the far side, so the shot goes through both lungs (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). Texas Parks and Wildlife says take it with a firearm only if you are sure of your aim: a miss to the rear is a gut shot.

blocks.p: Swipe sideways to see the whole table.

head: Animal facing
Take it?
rows: Broadside (side-on)
Yes: the best shot, firearm or bow (Texas Parks and Wildlife)
Quartering away
Yes, aiming at the far shoulder (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife); with a firearm only if you are sure of your aim (Texas Parks and Wildlife)
Quartering toward you
Pass it up. More likely to hit the shoulder bone, and the deer can see you move; never with a bow (Texas Parks and Wildlife, Massachusetts bowhunter education)
Facing you head-on
Pass it up. It can ruin a lot of meat and go through the stomach; never with a bow (Texas Parks and Wildlife)
Facing away, rear end toward you
Never: no large vital area shows (Texas Parks and Wildlife, Alaska Department of Fish and Game)
Head
Never: a low-percentage shot (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife)
Straight down from a tree stand
Never. Wait until the deer is at least 10 yards (9 m) out and broadside or quartering away (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife)

list: From a tree stand, a steep shot may go through only one lung, and the animal can go a long way before it dies (Massachusetts bowhunter education). A deer can live with one lung, and the backbone blocks much of the vital area from above (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Most missed or wounded game comes from bad decisions: rushing, shooting too far, or shooting at a bad angle. Pass on a difficult shot (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

blocks.p: Alaska Department of Fish and Game shows quartering-toward and head-on shots, says to consider how the angle moves the vital organs, and to be sure your bullet can break any bones in the way. This app goes by the more cautious sources: pass up quartering-toward and head-on shots.

steps: Reload, and keep watching the deer: a wounded deer can hurt you (Missouri Department of Conservation).
Watch where it runs and listen for it to fall. Crashing sounds usually mean a fatal hit and a short trail (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission).
Mark in your mind where it stood when you shot and the last place you saw it. Take a compass bearing to that spot and estimate the distance (Massachusetts hunter education).
Note the time, and stay where you are (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

When the wait is over, go to where the deer stood and look for blood, hair, scuffed ground, broken twigs and your arrow (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). Check the ground and the trail before you decide you missed (Maine hunter education).

sections.h: How long to wait before you follow

blocks.p: A deer that is pushed while it is still alive often runs off and is never found (Massachusetts hunter education). Unless you can see the deer down, wait before you follow it.
Swipe sideways to see the whole table.

head: Blood and sign
Usually means
Wait
rows: Pink or bright red and frothy
Lung hit (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission)
At least 1 hour (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife)
Bright red, not frothy
Heart or a cut artery (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission)
At least 1 hour (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife)
Dark red
Muscle or liver hit. A liver-hit deer may live longer (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife)
1 hour or more (North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission); no source opened gives a firmer figure
Dark, with brown or green plant matter
Gut shot (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission)
At least 6 to 8 hours (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife)

list: Massachusetts hunter education waits 30 minutes after a firearm shot and 1 hour after an arrow, and longer if you are unsure of the shot; Maine hunter education says half an hour to an hour. New Jersey Fish and Wildlife waits 1 hour before following any ordinary hit. This app goes by at least 1 hour.
A gut-shot deer may go into a swamp, creek or pond to cool down: check the water nearby (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

steps: Walk beside the trail, not on it, so you don’t wipe out the sign (North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission, New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Look for blood on the ground and on leaves and brush above the ground, and for hair, bone, tracks, broken twigs and scattered leaves (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, Maine hunter education).
Mark the trail as you go with bright orange flagging, so you can find your way back to the last sign. Take the flagging down afterwards (Maine hunter education, Massachusetts hunter education).
Keep the group small: three people at most (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). More eyes help in poor light or bad weather (North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission).
Wounded deer often take the easiest way, downhill and toward water (Massachusetts hunter education, Maine hunter education).

If you lose the trail, go back to the last sign and search outward in widening circles (Massachusetts hunter education, New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). Be ready for a follow-up shot (North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission).
If you jump the deer from its bed, leave quietly so you don’t push it further (Massachusetts hunter education).
Stop hunting and search for any animal you wounded (Maine hunter education). Darkness or weather can stop you: the flagging lets you pick the trail up again the next day (Maine hunter education).
Watch it from a distance for breathing (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Approach from behind its head and stay away from its feet and antlers (Missouri Department of Conservation, Massachusetts hunter education).

The eyes of a dead deer are normally open (Massachusetts hunter education). Touch the corner of the eye with a long stick: if it blinks, it is still alive (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, Missouri Department of Conservation).
Still alive: finish it with a shot into the heart and lungs, only if that shot is legal (New York rules) and safe (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, Massachusetts hunter education).
Put your firearm or bow down only when you are certain the deer is dead (Missouri Department of Conservation).
Tag it if the law requires (New York rules), then field dress it as soon as you can (Massachusetts hunter education).

blocks.warn: NYS DEC counted 11 falls from tree stands in New York in 2024, two of them fatal; in nine the hunter wore no safety harness or had not connected it to the tree. DEC says a fall-arrest harness kept connected to the tree could have prevented all of them.

steps: Read the stand maker’s instructions and warnings. Check the stand, straps and chains every season, replace worn or missing parts, and don’t leave a stand up all year (NYS DEC).

Wear a full-body harness with a lifeline, fixed at the base of the tree and to the tree just above your head when you sit. Connect your harness to the lifeline with a carabiner and a prusik knot, which slides along it (NYS DEC).
Connect to the tree before your feet leave the ground and stay connected until you are back down (NYS DEC).
The harness needs a foot strap: hanging in a harness cuts off blood in your legs (suspension trauma), and the strap takes the pressure off (NYS DEC).

Never climb in or out of a stand with a loaded firearm (NYS DEC). Once you are safely in the stand, raise your gear on a haul line: the firearm unloaded and muzzle down, the haul line never tied to the trigger or trigger guard; a bow or crossbow with its quiver (NYS DEC).
Keep a knife, phone, flashlight and whistle in your pockets, not in a pack hanging in the tree (NYS DEC).

blocks.p: Someone fell? Check them in order with the trauma check, and use the protocols for what you find.

list: Hypothermia happens when your body loses heat faster than it makes it. Cold, wet conditions bring it on, and it can happen at up to about 50°F (10°C) (Maine hunter education).
Sweat, rain and dew on brush slowly soak your clothes; wind takes heat away as it dries you; resting against a cold surface pulls heat out of you (Maine hunter education).

Dress properly, stay out of dangerous weather, and dry off quickly when you get wet (Maine hunter education). Layers that wick sweat, no cotton, and a wind- and water-resistant outer layer (NYS DEC, ice fishing).
High-calorie food such as chocolate, peanuts or raisins gives quick energy that helps your body make heat (Maine hunter education).
Cold weather narrows blood vessels and adds to the strain on the heart (American Heart Association).

blocks.warn: Dragging an animal through the woods can leave even a fit hunter breathless and could bring on a heart attack or stroke (American Heart Association). Take breaks. Don’t hurt yourself dragging something too heavy for you: go and get help (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).

list: Drag or cart the deer out; don’t carry it on your shoulders, where another hunter could take it for a live deer (Missouri Department of Conservation). Put hunter orange on it (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Drag a buck by its antlers. For a doe or a fawn, make a handle with a strong stick between the hind legs at the hocks. A deer cart saves your back (Missouri Department of Conservation).

A smaller field-dressing cut keeps dirt out while you drag (Cornell Cooperative Extension). Avoid dragging through water or dirt (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife). Wrap the carcass in a cloth to keep dirt and flies off (Missouri Department of Conservation).
Keep it as clean and cool as you can on the way home (Missouri Department of Conservation). Cooling is in Field dressing game.

blocks.p: Chest pain, or a drooping face, a weak arm or slurred speech while dragging? Stop and use the protocol.

list: Shot placement matters even more: the best shot is just behind the front shoulder, with the bear angled slightly away from broadside. Take extra time, calm down and slow your breathing before you shoot (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
A bear’s fur is long and thick: take that into account and find the heart and lungs precisely. A wounded bear can be dangerous (Connecticut hunter safety manual).
The waiting, trailing and approach above are the general hunter education steps; no source opened gives separate ones for bear.

blocks.warn: Bear meat can carry trichinella worms. How to cook it, and why bear is never made into jerky, are in Field dressing game and Keeping game meat.

blocks.p: Someone shot, or cut while dressing game? Use the protocols.

Making sure the deer is dead, gutting it, cooling it and the signs that an animal is not safe to eat are in Field dressing game. Cutting it up is in Butchering deer and small game; how long it keeps, and how to keep it, in Keeping game meat.
